body:
OBJECTIVES
- Students sequence the major events of the Cold War and after, and explain the policy of containment (D2.His.14.9-12, D2.His.2.9-12).
- Students analyze change and continuity in American foreign policy through four presidential sources from 1947 to 1987 (D2.His.2.9-12, D2.Civ.3.9-12, RH.9-10.9).
- Students trace a current public issue to its historical roots, evaluate policy options by their intended and unintended consequences, and propose informed action through deliberation (D4.6.9-12, D4.7.9-12, D4.8.9-12, D2.Civ.13.9-12).
- Students write a semester synthesis argument about citizenship and the role of government from industrialization to the present (D2.His.16.9-12, D4.1.9-12).

MATERIALS
- Readings in the activities: Cold War timeline, the Truman Doctrine, Eisenhower's farewell, Kennedy's inaugural, Reagan at the Brandenburg Gate
- Students' sourcing charts and essays from the whole semester (for the final assessment)
- Contact information for local officials (city council, school board, state legislators) for the civic proposals
- Note: keep the civic project nonpartisan. Students choose the issue and the position; your role is to require evidence, fair treatment of other views, and respectful deliberation.

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read Pay Any Price. Lesson activity: The Cold War in Twelve Events. Build a class timeline and discuss which events made the Cold War hot (Korea, Vietnam) and which nearly did (the Cuban Missile Crisis).
Day 2: Four Presidents, One Cold War: read Truman, Eisenhower, Kennedy and Reagan; students chart what stays the same and what changes. Begin the analysis.
Day 3: Launch Take Informed Action. Students choose an issue with roots in this course (for example: worker pay and unions, food and product safety, voting access, free speech and surveillance in times of crisis, school equity), write a compelling question, and find sources.
Day 4: Deliberation day: in small groups, students present their issue and options; the group uses a structured deliberation (each option's benefits, costs and who bears them) and records points of agreement. Proposals are due in a week.
Day 5: Semester assessment: Citizenship and Government, 1840 to Today (no AI help; students may use their notes and readings).

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: offer a menu of four pre-researched issues with two sources each, and a proposal template (issue, history, options, recommendation, action step).
- Support: for the semester synthesis, students may outline with a partner first, and may use their sourcing charts.
- Extension: students deliver their proposal to a real audience, such as public comment at a school board meeting, and reflect afterward on what happened.
- Extension: compare Eisenhower's warning with defense spending as a share of the economy then and now, using federal data.
- Multilingual learners (ELL): students may present the civic proposal orally or bilingually, and may choose an issue that affects their home community. Provide frames: "One option is ___. It would help ___, but it might ___."

FAMILY NOTE (send home at the start of the unit)
We are finishing the semester with the Cold War and recent American history, and with a civic project. Each student will choose a current issue, trace it back through the history we have studied, and propose a specific action, such as a letter to a local official. Students choose their own issue and position. Please ask your student which issue they chose and why. Thank you for a wonderful semester of history.
title: Teacher guide: The Cold War and Modern America
